name: Social Recon 101
description: We found a suspicious user handle '@GhostAdmin99'. Read through the attached text file to find their digital footprint and the first flag.

name: The GitHub Leak
description: The target deleted their code, but we managed to scrape a leaked commit note! Decode this Base64 string to see what they were hiding:

name: Forum Secrets
description: We found a deleted post on an underground hacker forum. The attacker used a ROT47 cipher to hide their text. Crack it:

name: Shadow Domain
description: We found a secret DNS record pointing to a hidden server! Download this intercepted DNS zone file and read carefully to spot the flag.

name: Inspect Element
description: A junior developer was feeling lazy and left a comment directly in the HTML code. Right-click this very dashboard, select 'Inspect', and look through the source code to find the hidden token!

name: Sneaky SQLi
description: Someone bypassed the login page using a SQL injection! Look through the attached web server logs to find the exact payload they used.

name: Server Pivot
description: After breaking into the website, the attacker tricked the server into making a request to the internal network (SSRF). Check the web logs again to find the flag they grabbed.

hints.text: Think about what a localhost IP address looks like. Is there a loopback address you can spot in the URL parameter?

name: Prototype Pollution
description: The web app handles user settings really poorly. We caught a malicious JSON payload the attacker sent to give themselves admin rights. Download the payload and grab the flag from it.

hints.text: In JavaScript, you can pollute the prototype by injecting into the __proto__ object.
Look closely at the JSON file. The attacker injected 'admin:true', but there is another property hidden right next to it.

name: Caesar's Salad
description: This text file contains a secret message. It looks like a random mess of letters, but it's just a classic Caesar cipher shifted by 13. Decrypt it!

name: Vigenère Key
description: This cipher is a bit tougher because it uses a repeating keyword. Crack the Vigenère cipher below and wrap your answer in tcs{} to get the flag.

name: Weak RSA
description: We found an encrypted message and a public RSA key in this file. The problem? The prime numbers they used are way too small! Factor them out to crack the encryption.

hints.text: You can use an online tool like FactorDB to break down the Modulus (N) into its P and Q factors instantly.

name: Hex to ASCII
description: We managed to extract this raw Hexadecimal string from the attacker's memory. Convert the Hex characters back into normal ASCII text to read the flag:

hints.text: Don't overthink this one. The string is already the flag, it's just encoded in Base16 (Hex).
Throw the string into CyberChef and use the 'From Hex' operation.

name: Magic Bytes
description: We found a PNG image file, but it refuses to open! The first few 'magic bytes' of the file header got corrupted. Fix them in a hex editor to see the image.

name: PCAP Carving
description: Two computers were talking on the network, and we recorded it in this PCAP file. Open it in Wireshark and figure out what secret file they were sending to each other.

name: Hidden in the Pixels
description: It looks like a normal picture, but we know there's data hiding inside the pixel colors! Analyze the stego image file to extract the hidden message.

name: Memory Dump
description: We took a snapshot of a compromised computer's RAM. We found a chunk of data inside the Windows password process (LSASS). Download the dump and find the flag.

hints.text: The dump is from Mimikatz processing the sekurlsa::logonpasswords command.
You are looking for the plaintext password belonging to the user 'Administrator'.
Open the text file and literally CTRL+F for the word 'Administrator' to find it.

name: Packet Snooping
description: Something weird is happening on the local network. Open up the provided PCAP file and dig through the raw packet data to find what the attacker injected.

name: BGP Hijack
description: Our internet traffic is being routed to the wrong place! Download this BGP routing log showing a fake network path. Can you spot the fake Autonomous System (AS)?

name: Ping Smuggling
description: The hacker snuck data right past the firewall by hiding it inside ping requests (ICMP). We grabbed the raw Hex bytes of the payload. Translate it to text to get the flag:

name: Secret DNS Chat
description: The malware is talking to the hacker by making fake DNS requests! Check out this command we caught. Decode the Base64 part to find the hidden flag:

name: RockYou Basics
description: Someone dumped a database, and we found an MD5 password hash in the text file. It's a super common password, so a simple dictionary attack should break it easily!

name: Adding Symbols
description: The user got smart and added symbols to their password. Crack this SHA256 hash, then put your answer inside the tcs{} format to submit it:

name: Local Dictionary
description: This user bases their passwords on their hometown. Crack this MD5 hash using some creative local keywords, then submit it in the tcs{} format:

name: NTLM Relay
description: We captured a Windows NTLMv2 hash while the attacker was moving across the network. Open the text file and find the admin password they were using.

name: Basic Strings
description: We found a suspicious program file. The developer made a huge mistake and typed the secret password right into the code! Extract the readable text to find the flag.

name: Reading Assembly
description: We broke the malware down into raw Assembly code. Read through the text file to figure out how the program jumps past the security check.

name: Unpacking UPX
description: The malware was packed tightly to hide its code. We dumped it out of the computer's memory while it was running. Download the memory snippet to grab the flag.

hints.text: Look closely at the memory address in the text file. The flag is written right next to it!

name: Custom Virtual Machine
description: The malware runs in its own weird virtual machine! We caught the commands it sent to the memory stack. Read this sequence backwards to build the flag:
evidence: PUSH '}'; PUSH 'd'; PUSH 'e'; PUSH 's'; PUSH 'r'; PUSH 'e'; PUSH 'v'; PUSH 'e'; PUSH 'r'; PUSH '_'; PUSH 'e'; PUSH 'd'; PUSH 'o'; PUSH 'c'; PUSH 'p'; PUSH 'o'; PUSH '{'; PUSH 's'; PUSH 'c'; PUSH 't';

hints.text: The memory stack operates on a LIFO (Last In, First Out) basis.
Get a piece of paper and literally write down the characters one by one starting from the very end of the sequence.

name: Android Manifest
description: We decompiled a sketchy Android app. Look inside the AndroidManifest.xml file to see if they accidentally exported a hidden activity to the public.

name: Hardcoded Keys
description: Rule #1 of app development: Never hardcode your API keys! We pulled the strings.xml file out of the decompiled APK. Download it and find the flag.

name: Insecure Broadcast
description: The Android app was shouting sensitive info to the whole phone! We intercepted a system broadcast log. Download it and grab the flag from the payload data.
